headline: Five Days to the New Moon, and the Point Is Coiling
subhead: Bass are holding tight to the boulders, jumbo blues are working the rips, and the first albie of the season is closer than it's been all summer.
body_markdown:
There's a specific feeling at the Point in early August, and if you've fished it as many years as I have, you know it the second you step onto the rocks before first light. The water's still warm — 69 degrees off the Lighthouse, holding steady — but the air's got that first hint of change in it, and the current feels like it's loading up for something. Five days out from the August 12 new moon, and Montauk is coiling. I don't mean that lightly. Every year around this window, the tidal range starts building, the rips sharpen, and the whole east end shifts gears. This year's no different, except maybe a little more obvious than usual.

The striper bite has been a holding pattern for weeks now, and that's not a complaint — it's just where we are in the calendar. Fish are still here, they're just doing what August bass do: sitting deep on structure during the day and working the current edges hard at night. The boulder field off the Point, that stretch between the Lighthouse and North Bar, has been giving up quality fish on the top of the incoming, right at first light. I had a guy sight-cast an eel into the white water last Thursday and connect on a 38-inch fish that buried itself in the rocks for a solid five minutes before we turned it. That's the kind of fish this stretch produces when the tide's right — not numbers, but the real deal. Bucktails in the 2- to 3-ounce range, white or olive, worked slow along bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing, have been the more consistent daytime play. Don't overwork it. Let the current do the work and just keep contact.

Shagwong Reef has been holding bluefish, and I mean real bluefish — 12, 14 pounds, the kind that used to be a Montauk given and lately have felt more like an event. They're sitting on bunker schools that have been pushing through Block Island Sound, and when those schools tighten up over the reef on a building tide, it gets loud fast — birds diving, bait skying, the whole show. Chunked bunker on wire leader has been the ticket for anchoring on them, but if you want to cast, a bomber or a big popper worked through the surface chaos will get bit just as hard. Turtle Cove's had some smaller blues mixed with schoolie bass working bait pushed into the corner on the last of the outgoing — good action if you've got kids in the boat and want bent rods without a long run.

Fluke's been a mixed bag, and I'll be honest about that. The drift off the south side beaches has produced some quality fish — four- and five-pounders on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, fished on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 30 to 40 feet — but you're working for them. Plenty of shorts mixed in, and some drifts you'll go twenty minutes without a knock. The better bite's been happening on the humps and drop-offs south of the Point where the bottom breaks up and holds bait, rather than the flat sand. If fluke's your priority this week, I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping you off the structure.

Now here's the part everybody's been asking about at the docks. We flagged this pattern building last week, and it's still lining up — squid have been pushing hard into Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound as that water climbs into the high 50s and low 60s, and that's the exact signal that precedes Montauk's rips turning on for false albacore and bonito. It hasn't happened yet. I want to be straight about that — nobody's boated an albie off the Point as of this week, and I'm not going to tell you otherwise. But the pieces are lining up almost textbook: warming current corridor, squid staging to the east, and a new moon five days out that's going to put some real muscle into these tides. If there's a year the switch flips right on schedule, this feels like it.

Offshore, the boats running out toward West Atlantis have been into yellowfin over 100 pounds, with white marlin showing and the occasional blue marlin in the spread — a strong summer bite holding steady on the warm water anchored out there. Bluefin eight to sixteen miles out have grown into better-class fish too, and the guys have shifted off the troll and onto jig and chunk now that those fish are sitting on bait rather than running it down. That's a good sign for everything closer to shore — when the bait's thick enough to hold bluefin that tight to the beach, it tends to trickle down into everything else feeding behind it.

Looking ahead, I'd focus the next few days on the current-driven spots — North Bar on the building tide, the boulder field at dawn, Shagwong when the bunker's thick — because that's where the bite's been most honest lately. And I'd keep one rod rigged light and ready for albies starting Monday. If the tidal range does what it usually does heading into a new moon, the rips around the Point are going to sharpen fast, and when that first fish shows, it's not going to give you much warning.
